messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Arjun’s eight-year-old son was admitted to the pediatric ICU with a rapidly worsening infection, the days that followed narrowed into fluorescent light, antiseptic air, and the mechanical rhythm of monitors. Arjun spent nights in a vinyl chair beside the bed, half-awake and listening for any change in the boy’s breathing. He still remembers being told to step aside for procedures, watching masked staff move quickly around his son while he stood uselessly at the edge of the room. What lodged most deeply was not a single dramatic moment but the repeated sense that catastrophe could arrive at any second and that he had to stay alert enough to catch it first. By the time his son recovered and came home, Arjun had the outward appearance of relief, but internally he had not left the hospital.

In the months afterward, certain moments pulled him back with unnerving force. The sharp smell of antiseptic in a clinic hallway, a routine medical examination of his own, even checking into a hotel for a work conference and realizing he would have to sleep alone all carried the same jolt. As an animator, he often worked long hours in a dim studio and occasionally traveled for production meetings; the first night away from home became especially difficult because being alone in an unfamiliar room felt too close to those nights beside his son’s hospital bed, except now there was no way to keep watch. When these situations arose, Arjun’s mind would immediately lurch into frantic effort. He would run through worst-case scenarios in detail, telling himself he needed to be prepared for the next emergency. He repeatedly asked his wife, doctors, or even coworkers whether he seemed all right, whether his son was really out of danger, whether missing some sign had become possible again. He also found himself circling angrily around thoughts of how to get even with the people he felt had failed his family during the hospitalization, replaying delays and perceived dismissals and imagining confrontations that might finally balance what had happened.

These habits did not settle him for long. The more Arjun rehearsed disaster, the more easily ordinary cues took on the force of warning. A mild disinfectant smell in an urgent care waiting room became almost unbearable because he had already spent the morning mentally staging scenes of collapse and medical crisis. Before his own checkups, he would lie awake imagining bad news, and by the time he entered the exam room his body was keyed up enough that the paper on the examination table, the blood pressure cuff, and the clinician’s brisk manner all felt charged. Nights alone became harder in the same way: in hotel rooms on business trips, he would scan for signs that something might go wrong at home, call or text repeatedly for reassurance, and mentally rehearse who to contact if his son became ill again. Those efforts left him more vigilant, not less, so the room itself began to feel unsafe simply because he was alone with his thoughts.

At home this has gradually changed family life. His wife has become used to late-night questions he already knows she cannot definitively answer—whether their son looked pale at dinner, whether a cough sounded different, whether they should book another appointment just to be sure. Arjun experiences these questions as necessary, almost responsible, yet he can see the fatigue in her face. At work he remains highly skilled, but on days when he has to attend a medical appointment or after he catches a hospital-like smell in the building, he loses hours to spiraling preparation and checking. He has also nursed a bitter internal ledger about the hospital stay, returning again and again to fantasies of exposing or punishing the staff he believes did not grasp how close his son came to dying. He recognizes that these thoughts do not lead anywhere, but he cannot seem to stop using them, as if staying angry might keep him from ever being that helpless again.

He came to treatment after turning down another out-of-town studio trip because the prospect of sleeping alone in a hotel felt intolerable. What frightened him most was not only the surge of panic in those moments, but the growing sense that his life was organizing itself around preventing another catastrophe he could neither predict nor control. He wants to be able to walk into a clinic, travel for work, or spend a night away without his mind immediately building disaster scenes. More than that, he hopes to stop living as though his son is still in that hospital bed, while fearing that if he lets his guard down for even a moment, something terrible will happen again.
